EPPC Scholar Comment Supporting Department of Veterans Affairs “Reproductive Health 
Services” Proposed Rule, Docket ID VA-2025-VHA-0073, RIN 2900-AS31 
 
Dear Secretary Collins: 
 
I write in strong support of the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) proposed rule 
“Reproductive Health Services,”1 which would stop the unlawful use of taxpayer funds for abortion. I 
am a Fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center (EPPC), Director of EPPC’s Administrative State 
Accountability Project, and former attorney at the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. 
After the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade and returned the issue of abortion “to the 
people and their elected representatives,”2 the Biden administration sought to unilaterally (and 
unlawfully) expand abortion access by reinterpreting federal laws to promote abortion.3 In the wake of 
Dobbs and at the behest of President Biden, the VA conveniently discovered never-before-found authority 
to advance the Biden administration’s pro-abortion political agenda. 
Ignoring federal law that prohibits the VA from providing abortion benefits, the Biden VA 
claimed in September 2022 that it could provide abortion counseling and abortions at VA hospitals and 
clinics in any state, for any reason, through all nine months of pregnancy, and regardless of any state 
abortion laws.4 The interim final rule (IFR) was eventually finalized in March 2024 “without changes.”5

I applaud the VA and the Trump administration for seeking to rescind the unlawful “Biden Rule” 
in full, stop taxpayer funding for abortion, and allow the VA to focus on real healthcare for veterans and 
their beneficiaries. 
My comments below draw on comments submitted to the VA on the IFR and to OIRA before 
finalization of the IFR and before publication of this proposed rule.6 For the reasons I explain below, I 
urge the VA to promptly finalize the proposed rule with some additional clarifications. 
I. 
The Biden Rule Was a Political Response to Dobbs 
In the wake of Dobbs and because of Dobbs,7 the VA sought to implement the Biden 
administration’s radical pro-abortion political agenda in disregard of the Supreme Court’s direction in 
Dobbs that the issue of abortion is returned “to the people and their elected representatives.”8 
I agree with the VA that the Biden Rule was based on politics, not science.9 The Biden Rule 
functionally allows abortion on demand until birth.10 It does not impose any gestational limits or limits on 
access to abortion for mental, emotional, social, familial, or economic “health” reasons.11 
Abortion is a matter of “vast … political significance.”12 As discussed below, Congress has not 
directed the VA to provide taxpayer-funded abortion benefits and has, in fact, explicitly prohibited the 
VA from providing abortion benefits. Nevertheless, the Biden VA sought to provide taxpayer-funded 
abortion benefits. This violates the major questions doctrine.13 
The Biden Rule’s claim of “good cause” for an IFR and “necessity” to provide abortion benefits 
“to protect the lives and health of veterans” was pretextual.14 The Biden VA’s real goal was to undermine 
state prolife laws after Dobbs. As the Biden Rule explained, “[a]fter Dobbs, certain States have begun to 
enforce existing abortion bans and restrictions on care, and are proposing and enacting new ones, creating

The VA’s claim of “urgent risks” to pregnant women was a lie. Tellingly the Biden VA failed to identify 
a single woman who had faced such risks in the three months between the Dobbs decision and its IFR or 
who would have faced such risks but for the abortion benefits provided by the VA in the year and a half 
before the rule was finalized. This is not surprising considering no state abortion law prohibits care to 
save a mother’s life, treatment for ectopic pregnancies, or miscarriage management.16 And for good 
reason. Care to save a mother’s life, as well as treatment for ectopic pregnancies and miscarriage 
management are not abortion. The VA’s brazen claims of urgent risks are further undermined by the fact 
that the number of women obtaining abortions from the VA was “significantly lower” than what the 
Biden VA had anticipated.17 
II. 
The Biden Rule Is Unlawful 
The VA has federal statutory authority to provide medical services that the VA Secretary 
determines are “needed” for veterans under 38 U.S.C. § 1710 and “medically necessary and appropriate” 
for CHAMPVA beneficiaries 38 U.S.C. § 1781, subject to certain limitations. One of those limitations, 
found in Section 106 of the Veterans Health Care Act of 1992, is for abortion.18 
At the heart of the Biden Rule is the argument is that Section 106 does not mean what it says. The 
Biden Rule also argues that abortion is “needed” and “medically necessary and appropriate.”  
The Biden VA and Department of Justice (DOJ) conveniently claimed post-Dobbs that the 
Veterans’ Health Care Eligibility Reform Act of 1996 (which does not mention Section 106 or abortion) 
“effectively overtook” Section 106 “by establishing a new standard to focus on medical necessity as ‘the 
sole criterion of eligibility for VA hospital care and medical services.’”19 But “effectively overtaken” is a 
novel legal standard the Supreme Court has never endorsed. 
The Biden Rule further claimed that even if Section 106 was not “effectively overtaken,” the 
exclusion was limited only to those services provided under Section 106. But this argument likewise fails.

The prefatory language in Section 106 (“In furnishing hospital care and medical services under chapter 17 
of title 38, United States Code”) clearly states that the limitations in that section (including the abortion 
exclusion) apply to all hospital care and medical services provided under chapter 17 of title 38, which 
includes services for veterans under 38 U.S.C. § 1710 and for CHAMPVA beneficiaries under 38 U.S.C. 
§ 1781. In sum, “the wholesale revision of Chapter 17 in 1996 and the specific limitations of section 106” 
does not “limit the continued force and effect of section 106.”20 
Further, even if Section 106 was ambiguous (it is not), after the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in 
Loper Bright the VA is not entitled to deference when it is interpreting federal law.21 Rather, the VA and 
courts are bound by the best reading of the text. Here, the best reading of Section 106 is that Congress has 
prohibited the VA from providing abortion benefits. Beyond the plain text, this understanding of Section 
106 is also supported by Congressional action, including Congress’ repeated decision (most recently in 
the One Big Beautiful Bill22) not to use taxpayer dollars to fund abortion.23 
The Biden Rule also runs afoul of other federal laws, including the Anti-Deficiency Act, the 
Assimilative Crimes Act, and the Comstock Act.24 In short, The VA’s authority to provide abortions is 
not just “dubious,” it is “nonexistent.” 25 
I agree with the VA that the VA’s “legal authority to ‘un-do’ the changes made in September 
2022 is beyond doubt.”26 I also agree that the VA’s proposal is “consistent with VA’s decades-long 
interpretation of the law” and that it “fully compl[ies]” with the abortion exclusion.27  
I urge the VA to explicitly state that the VA does not have authority under Section 106 to 
provide abortion benefits. Though the VA “need not reach that decision” in its rule,28 this separate and 
independent reason for excluding abortion only bolsters the VA’s rule—the Secretary has not only 
determined (rightly) that abortion is not needed or appropriate, but the VA is statutorily prohibited from 
providing abortion benefits. Taking this firm and legally defensible stance will help ensure that the 
Trump administration’s policies outlast the Trump administration and cannot be easily reversed when a 
different VA Secretary determines that abortion is needed and appropriate. 
III. 
Rescinding the Biden Rule Aligns with the Trump Administration’s Priorities 
The Biden Rule was a political response to the Supreme Court’s decision in Dobbs and state 
laws protecting unborn children. Rescinding the Biden Rule squarely aligns with President Trump’s 
priorities and the following executive actions.

Campaign Promise. Rescinding the Biden Rule would advance President Trump’s campaign 
promise to allow states to regulate abortion and protect unborn human life.29 The Biden Rule raised 
federalism concerns, including whether state abortion laws would be preempted and whether state health 
and safety laws would be respected by federal employees.30 
Executive Order 14182: Enforcing the Hyde Amendment. On January 24, 2025, President Trump 
signed an executive order “to end the forced use of Federal taxpayer dollars to fund or promote elective 
abortion.”31 The executive order showed that: 
Congress has annually enacted ... laws that prevent Federal funding of elective abortion, 
reflecting a longstanding consensus that American taxpayers should not be forced to pay for that 
practice. However, the previous administration disregarded this established, commonsense policy 
by embedding forced taxpayer funding of elective abortions in a wide variety of Federal 
programs.32 
One of those federal programs is VA health benefits. Rescinding the Biden Rule will eliminate taxpayer 
funding of abortion by the VA. 
Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Enforces Overwhelmingly Popular Demand to Stop 
Taxpayer Funding of Abortion. A fact sheet on Executive Order 14182 reiterated that Congress’ intent 
via the laws it passes is to “protect taxpayers from being forced to pay for abortion.”33 The fact sheet 
specifically stated that “the previous administration embedded federal funding of elective abortion in a 
wide variety of government programs” and emphasized President Trump’s desire to return the issue of 
abortion to the states, which includes addressing the “federal overreach and taxpayer dollars” going to 
“the Department of Veterans Affairs allow[ing] hospitals to provide abortions.”34 
The fact sheet also stated that the federal government “will no longer force violations of faith 
and conscience or impede the ability of states to determine life policies through a vote of the 
people.”35 The Biden Rule was mentioned right after this position.

Rescinding the Biden Rule supports President Trump’s efforts to stop taxpayer funding of 
abortion and align VA policy with a robust understanding of conscience and religious freedom rights 
so that no medical professional, hospital, or federal employee is forced to violate their deeply held 
religious beliefs by ending the life of an unborn human through abortion. 
Executive Order 14217: Commencing the Reduction of the Federal Bureaucracy. One of 
President Trump’s priorities stated in this executive order is to “reduc[e] the scope of the Federal 
bureaucracy” and “minimize Government waste and abuse.”38 “[R]educing government overreach” is 
one of the considerations mentioned, which aligns with President Trump’s desire to stop taxpayer 
funding of abortion. 
Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Continues the Reduction of the Federal Bureaucracy. 
The fact sheet accompanying EO 14217 stated that “by reducing the Federal footprint, [the 
administration] is returning power to local communities and state governments.”39 Rescinding the 
Biden Rule is consistent with this policy priority by eliminating federal funds used for abortion and 
returning the issue of abortion to the states. 
Executive Order 14219: Ensuring Lawful Governance And Implementing The President’s 
“Department Of Government Efficiency” Deregulatory Initiative. This executive order stated that it is 
the policy of the Trump administration to “focus the executive branch’s limited enforcement resources 
on regulations squarely authorized by constitutional Federal statutes” and that it is a priority of the 
administration to restore “the constitutional separation of powers.”40 The order flagged classes of 
regulations that should be rescinded, including regulations that are not based on “the best reading of the 
underlying statutory authority or prohibition,” are “not authorized by clear statutory authority,” and 
“implicate matters of social, political, or economic significance.”41 Rescinding the Biden Rule, which is 
contrary to federal statutes, implicates abortion, and raises federalism concerns, falls squarely within 
these policy priorities.

Executive Order 14168: Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring

the policy of the United States to recognize two sexes, male and female. These sexes are not changeable

“pregnant individual” 41 times in the 24-page rule.45 Consistent with the order’s recognition that there 
are only two sexes, this rule rightly recognizes the biological reality that only females can get pregnant 
and uses terms like “pregnant women.”46 
IV. 
Abortion Is Not “Needed” or “Appropriate” Healthcare 
I agree with the VA that abortion is not a “needed” service for veterans and not “medically 
necessary and appropriate” for CHAMPVA beneficiaries.47 
 
In the Biden VA’s zeal to promote abortion at all costs, the Biden Rule ignored the harms of 
abortion to both unborn children and their mothers, relying instead on general claims of need that did not 
exist and alleged benefits that did not materialize.48 
 
Abortion is not healthcare. Abortion ends the life of an innocent child and harms women. In April 
2025, EPPC released the largest-known study of how the abortion pill harms women, based on an 
unprecedented analysis of real-world insurance data.49 Significantly, the study found that “10.93 percent 
of women experience sepsis, infection, hemorrhaging, or another serious or life-threatening adverse event 
within 45 days following a mifepristone abortion.50 This is “far greater than the summary figure of ‘less 
than 0.5 percent’ in clinical trials reported on the drug label.”51 In the dataset, from 2017 to 2023, the 
average cost for mifepristone abortion and treatment for associated adverse events was $1,192 overall, 
including $3,936 in cases where there was at least one serious adverse event.52 
Rescinding the Biden Rule will turn these harms and costs of the Biden Rule into benefits of the 
Trump rule when finalized. There will be health benefits to women who would have otherwise

I applaud the Trump VA for seeking “to ensure it is appropriately prioritizing and addressing the 
urgent need to protect and preserve the lives of both the mother and the unborn child.”53 Unlike in the 
Biden Rule, caution should be exercised in weighing the monetary costs of an abortion against the costs 
of care for a mother and her newborn. There is no compelling interest in the intentional taking of an 
innocent human life in the womb, even if it costs less than providing medical care.54 
I agree with the VA that the Trump rule’s benefits exceed any costs. As the VA recognizes, 
rescinding the Biden Rule, will restore the VA to “its proper role as the United States’ provider of needed 
medical services to those who served, delivered on behalf of a grateful nation.”55 As EPPC’s comment on 
the Biden Rule explained, abortion disadvantages women and women don’t need abortion to succeed.56 
V. 
The Trump Rule Should Provide Additional Clarity 
Scope of Abortion. I agree with the VA that “claims in the prior administration’s rule that 
abortions throughout pregnancy are needed to save the lives of pregnant women are incorrect. The lives 
of pregnant women will continue to be protected without regard for the previous administration’s rule.”57 
This is true because miscarriage management, treatment for an ectopic pregnancy, and procedures to save 
the life of the mother are not an abortion. Because miscarriage management, treatment for an ectopic 
pregnancy, and procedures to save the life of the mother are not an abortion, they are not implicated by 
the abortion exclusion in Section 106 or the VA’s regulations. Nevertheless, some seem to not know (or 
intentionally misstate) which services qualify as an abortion. 
I urge the VA to be clear that miscarriage management, treatment for an ectopic 
pregnancy, and procedures to save the life of the mother are not an abortion and thus are not 
implicated by the abortion exclusions. Being explicit about what is not an abortion provides clarity and 
bolsters the VA’s legal position against any legal challenges to its rule. 
Abortion Exclusion Exception. Currently, the VA is proposing to return to the pre-2022 
regulatory language. This means veterans’ medical benefits package has an exclusion for abortions and 
abortion counseling and CHAMPVA benefits have an exclusion for abortions, “except when a physician 
certifies that the life of the mother would be endangered if the fetus were carried to term,” and for 
abortion counseling.58 
I have several concerns with the language in the CHAMPVA exception to the abortion exclusion. 
First, life-saving care is not an abortion, but the way this exclusion is worded suggests otherwise. Second, 
the undefined terms “endangered” and “life of the mother” open the door to bad faith compliance. 
Because all pregnancies and childbirth inherently have some risk to a mother’s life, a physician could 
claim that any pregnancy endangers the life of a mother warranting an abortion. Third, this exception is 
not included in the veterans’ regulatory provision, suggesting either that lifesaving care for a pregnant

To remedy these concerns and provide clarity, I ask the VA to eliminate the exception 
language in the CHAMPVA regulation, or at a minimum, reword the exception to reflect that life-
saving care is not an abortion, eliminate the possibility of bad faith compliance, and provide 
adequate care to a woman. 
Some may claim that the exception language is necessary in general or as it is currently worded 
because the VA is required to provide the “same or similar” benefits to CHAMPVA beneficiaries as the 
DOD provides under TRICARE.59 TRICARE currently contains the same exception (and also includes 
exceptions for the cases of rape and incest).60 Because lifesaving care is not an abortion, regardless of 
whether CHAMPVA regulations include the exception phrase, lifesaving care for pregnant women is not 
excluded—the same as TRICARE. Excluding all abortion benefits complies with the VA’s statutory 
obligations because it is similar to TRICARE’s exclusion of abortion benefits except in the limited cases 
of rape or incest. 
No Additional Exceptions. Some have suggested that the VA should instead add more exceptions 
to the abortion exclusions for the cases of rape and incest. But doing so would pose several legal 
problems. First, Section 106 prohibits providing abortion benefits regardless of the circumstances of 
conception. Second, providing abortion benefits in such cases would raise issues around federalism and 
preemption of state laws that prohibit abortion in those cases.61 Third, providing such an exception would 
require a determination by the VA Secretary that it is “necessary” and “appropriate” to kill children who 
were conceived through no fault of their own in such unfortunate circumstances.62 Fourth, requiring VA 
employees to provide abortions and abortion counseling even in limited circumstances would raise 
conscience and religious freedom concerns.63  The VA should clarify that it cannot provide any 
abortions or abortion counseling even in cases of rape or incest because the VA does not have legal 
authority to do so.

Conclusion 
For the reasons stated above, the VA should promptly finalize the rule with the suggested 
clarifications. Rescinding the Biden Rule and ending the VA’s taxpayer funding of abortion implements
